bubble-sort.worstCaseTrigger: Reverse-sorted input: every comparison swaps, pass k makes n - k comparisons, and the total is n(n-1)/2. Sorted input stops after one pass with no swaps, O(n); random input still needs about n²/4 swaps, so the average stays O(n²).
bubble-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(1): it sorts in place with one temporary for the swap, and there is no recursion.

contrast.point: also O(n²) and in place, but far fewer writes on nearly sorted input

defend.time: why Bubble Sort is O(n²) on reverse-sorted input
defend.remedy: how the early-exit check makes sorted input O(n)
defend.space: why it needs only O(1) extra space

selection-sort.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse than another: every pass scans the whole unsorted region for its minimum, so it always makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons, sorted or not. Best, average and worst are all O(n²).
selection-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(1): in place, with one swap per pass.

contrast.point: adapts to sorted input in O(n), which Selection Sort cannot, though Selection Sort makes at most n - 1 swaps

defend.time: why Selection Sort is O(n²) even on sorted input
defend.alternative: why it still makes at most n - 1 swaps
defend.space: what extra space it needs

insertion-sort.worstCaseTrigger: Reverse-sorted input: each key shifts past every element before it, about n²/2 shifts. Sorted input shifts nothing, O(n); on random input each key moves about halfway back, so the average is still O(n²).
insertion-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(1): in place, holding only the current key.

contrast.point: O(n log n) on every input, at the cost of O(n) extra memory

defend.time: why Insertion Sort is O(n²) on reverse-sorted input but O(n) on sorted input
defend.space: what extra space it needs

merge-sort.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse than another: the array halves about log n times and every level merges all n elements, so best, average and worst are all O(n log n).
merge-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the merge buffer, plus O(log n) stack frames for the recursion depth.

contrast.point: the same average time in place with an O(log n) stack, but an O(n²) worst case

defend.time: why Merge Sort is O(n log n) on every input
defend.space: why it needs O(n) extra memory and how deep its recursion goes

quick-sort.worstCaseTrigger: Sorted or reverse-sorted input with this last-element pivot: each partition peels off one element, so there are n levels of about n comparisons, O(n²). On random input the pivot splits near the middle on average, giving about log n levels and O(n log n).
quick-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(log n) for the stack of pending ranges (the recursion) when splits are balanced, O(n) when every split is lopsided; partitioning itself is in place.

contrast.point: guaranteed O(n log n), but O(n) extra memory

defend.time: why Quick Sort degrades to O(n²)
defend.remedy: how a randomised or median-of-three pivot prevents it
defend.space: what space the recursion costs

shell-sort.worstCaseTrigger: It depends on the gap sequence: with the halving gaps used here, some inputs still force about n² moves, O(n²). Better sequences reach about O(n log² n) or O(n^1.5); nearly sorted input finishes quickly.
shell-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(1): it sorts in place, holding one value while shifting.

contrast.point: the gap-1 pass alone, O(n²) on reverse-sorted input

defend.time: why Shell Sort beats insertion sort and what its gap sequence does to the worst case
defend.space: what extra space it needs

heap-sort.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: building the heap is O(n), and each of the n extractions sifts down at most log n levels, so O(n log n) on every input.
heap-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(1): the heap lives in the array being sorted.

contrast.point: also O(n log n) on every input, and stable, but needs O(n) extra memory

defend.time: why Heap Sort is O(n log n) on every input
defend.alternative: what it gives up against Merge Sort
defend.space: why it needs only O(1) extra space

counting-sort.worstCaseTrigger: A wide range of values: the count array has one slot per possible value k, so time and space are O(n + k), which is slow when k is much larger than n. No input order is worse than another.
counting-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(n + k): the count array of size k plus an output array of size n.

contrast.point: comparison-based, O(n log n) whatever the range of values

defend.time: why Counting Sort is O(n + k) without comparing elements
defend.alternative: when the range k makes it worse than a comparison sort
defend.space: what space the count and output arrays take

radix-sort.worstCaseTrigger: Many digits: it makes one stable pass per digit, k passes of O(n + b) for b buckets (10 for decimal), so O(nk) with the base fixed; longer numbers mean more passes. Input order does not matter.
radix-sort.auxiliarySpace: O(n + b): one digit's b buckets plus an output array.

contrast.point: one pass over the whole value range, O(n + k), impractical when values are large

defend.time: why Radix Sort is O(nk) for k-digit numbers
defend.alternative: why each digit pass must be stable
defend.space: what space each pass needs

linear-search.worstCaseTrigger: The target is last or absent: every one of the n elements is checked. At best it is first, O(1); on average about n/2 checks, still O(n).

contrast.point: O(log n), but only on sorted data

defend.time: why Linear Search is O(n) when the target is missing
defend.alternative: when Binary Search would be faster and what it requires
defend.space: what extra space it uses

binary-search.worstCaseTrigger: The target is absent: each comparison halves the range, so it takes about log2 n + 1 comparisons before the range is empty. The average is also O(log n), because most positions are only reached after nearly every halving.
binary-search.auxiliarySpace: O(1) iteratively (low, high and mid); a recursive version adds O(log n) stack frames.

contrast.point: works on unsorted data, but needs O(n)

defend.time: why Binary Search needs only O(log n) comparisons
defend.alternative: why the array must be sorted for that to hold
defend.space: what space the iterative and recursive versions need

bst.worstCaseTrigger: Inserting values in sorted order: each goes to the right of the last, so the tree becomes a chain and an operation walks O(n) nodes. Random insert order keeps the height near log n, so the average is O(log n).
bst.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the nodes; an operation needs O(1) extra iteratively, or O(h) stack frames recursively, where h is the height.

contrast.point: rebalances with rotations so the height stays O(log n) for any insert order

defend.time: why a binary search tree is O(log n) when balanced but O(n) when values arrive sorted
defend.remedy: how a self-balancing tree such as AVL prevents it
defend.space: what memory the tree and a recursive operation use

bst-search.worstCaseTrigger: Each comparison moves one level down, so a search costs one root-to-leaf path, O(h). Values inserted in sorted order build a chain, h = n, so the worst case is O(n); a tree built from a random insert order has expected height about 2 ln n, so the average is O(log n).
bst-search.auxiliarySpace: O(1) iteratively; a recursive search holds one stack frame per level, O(h), which is O(n) on a chain.

contrast.point: a guaranteed O(log n) on a sorted array with no tree at all, but each insert into that array costs O(n) shifting, which a balanced tree avoids

defend.time: why searching a BST is O(log n) on average but O(n) when values were inserted in sorted order
defend.alternative: what binary search on a sorted array gives and loses by comparison
defend.space: what space a recursive search needs

bst-delete.worstCaseTrigger: Finding the node walks one root-to-leaf path, O(h); with two children, finding the in-order successor continues down the same subtree, still within O(h). So a delete is O(h): O(log n) on average for a randomly built tree, O(n) on a chain built from sorted values. The case (leaf, one child, two children) changes the constant work, not the bound.
bst-delete.auxiliarySpace: O(1) iteratively (the node, its parent and the successor); a recursive delete uses O(h) stack frames, O(n) on a chain.

contrast.point: the same three cases followed by rebalancing on the way up, so the height, and every delete, stays O(log n) guaranteed

defend.time: why deleting from a BST is O(h), even when the node has two children
defend.alternative: why a tree built from sorted values makes that O(n), which a self-balancing tree prevents
defend.space: what space the delete needs

tree-inorder.worstCaseTrigger: Every node is visited exactly once and each visit does O(1) work, so O(n) on any tree: no shape is worse for time, and the average is the same. Shape only changes the space.
tree-inorder.auxiliarySpace: O(h) for the recursion (or the explicit stack this run shows), where h is the height: about log n for a balanced tree, but n for a skewed one, such as a BST built from sorted values.

contrast.point: O(1) extra space, by temporarily threading right pointers back to ancestors, at the cost of modifying the tree during the walk

defend.time: why an in-order traversal is O(n) whatever the shape of the tree
defend.space: why its stack is O(h), which only reaches O(n) on a skewed tree

tree-preorder.worstCaseTrigger: Every node is visited exactly once and each visit does O(1) work, so O(n) on any tree: no shape is worse for time, and the average is the same. Shape only changes the space.
tree-preorder.auxiliarySpace: O(h) for the recursion (or the explicit stack this run shows), where h is the height: about log n for a balanced tree, but n for a skewed one.

contrast.point: the same O(n) time, but its queue holds a whole level, about n/2 nodes at the bottom of a complete tree, where pre-order holds one root-to-leaf path

defend.time: why a pre-order traversal is O(n) whatever the shape of the tree
defend.space: why it needs O(h) stack space, which only reaches O(n) on a skewed tree

tree-postorder.worstCaseTrigger: Every node is visited exactly once, after both of its subtrees, and each visit does O(1) work, so O(n) on any tree: no shape is worse for time, and the average is the same. Shape only changes the space.
tree-postorder.auxiliarySpace: O(h) for the recursion (or the explicit stack this run shows), where h is the height: about log n for a balanced tree, but n for a skewed one.

contrast.point: the same O(n) time, but a queue as wide as the widest level instead of a stack as deep as the tree: less memory on a deep, narrow tree and more on a wide, shallow one

defend.time: why a post-order traversal is O(n) even though each node waits for both subtrees
defend.space: why its stack is O(h), which only reaches O(n) on a skewed tree

tree-level-order.spaceNote: queue holds one level, w = max width
tree-level-order.worstCaseTrigger: Every node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, O(1) each, so O(n) on any tree: no shape is worse for time, and the average is the same. Shape only changes the space.
tree-level-order.auxiliarySpace: O(w) for the queue, where w is the widest level: about n/2 leaves at the bottom of a complete tree, so O(n), but only O(1) for a chain.

contrast.point: the same O(n) time with an O(h) stack instead, small for a wide balanced tree and large for a deep chain: the opposite trade-off

defend.time: why level-order traversal is O(n)
defend.space: why its queue grows with the widest level, up to about n/2 nodes

avl-insert.spaceNote: call stack, height is always O(log n)

avl-delete.spaceNote: call stack, height is always O(log n)

rb-insert.spaceNote: call stack, height is always O(log n)

rb-delete.spaceNote: call stack, height is always O(log n)

max-heap-insert.bestNote: new value already satisfies the property

min-heap-insert.bestNote: new value already satisfies the property

trie-insert.worstNote: m = word length, independent of trie size

trie-search.worstNote: m = word length, independent of trie size

trie-delete.worstNote: m = word length, independent of trie size

bfs.worstCaseTrigger: Every vertex is enqueued once and every edge examined once (twice in an undirected graph), so O(V + E) on any graph: no input is worse, only larger.
bfs.auxiliarySpace: O(V) for the queue and the visited set; the queue can hold a whole level at once.

contrast.point: the same O(V + E), with a stack as deep as the longest path instead of a queue as wide as a level

defend.time: why BFS is O(V + E)
defend.alternative: why it finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph and DFS does not
defend.space: how large the queue can grow

dfs.worstCaseTrigger: Each vertex is visited once and each edge examined once, so O(V + E) on any graph: no input is worse, only larger.
dfs.auxiliarySpace: O(V) for the visited set, and the stack (or recursion) can reach depth V along a long path.

contrast.point: the same O(V + E), with a queue as wide as a level instead of a stack as deep as a path

defend.time: why DFS is O(V + E)
defend.space: how deep the stack or recursion can go, and when that becomes a problem

dijkstra.worstCaseTrigger: This implementation finds the next closest node by scanning every unvisited node, O(V) for each of V steps, and relaxes each edge once: O(V² + E) on any graph. A binary heap makes each extraction and update O(log V), giving O((V + E) log V), which wins on sparse graphs.
dijkstra.auxiliarySpace: O(V) for the distance and parent tables and the visited set; a heap version adds up to O(E) heap entries.

contrast.point: handles negative edge weights, at O(V × E)

defend.time: why Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V)
defend.alternative: what changes if you use an array instead

grid-bfs.worstNote: no path exists - full grid explored

grid-dfs.worstNote: no path exists - full grid explored

grid-astar.averageNote: far fewer cells than Dijkstra, heuristic-guided
grid-astar.worstNote: no path exists - degrades toward Dijkstra

maze-kruskal.bestNote: always - α is the near-constant inverse Ackermann function

stack.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: push and pop touch only the top, so each is O(1) however many items are stored.
stack.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the items; each operation needs O(1) extra.

contrast.point: also O(1) per operation, but first in, first out instead of last in, first out

defend.time: why push and pop are O(1) whatever the size of the stack
defend.space: what space the stack uses as it grows

queue.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: enqueue touches only the rear and dequeue only the front, so each is O(1). A plain array that shifted everything left on dequeue would be O(n).
queue.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the items; each operation needs O(1) extra.

contrast.point: also O(1) per operation, but last in, first out

defend.time: why enqueue and dequeue are O(1)
defend.alternative: what goes wrong if dequeue shifts an array left
defend.space: what space the queue uses

circular-queue.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: front and rear advance with modulo capacity, so enqueue and dequeue are O(1) and nothing ever shifts.
circular-queue.auxiliarySpace: O(capacity), fixed up front, however many items are in it.

contrast.point: a linear array queue either shifts on dequeue, O(n), or wastes the slots it has passed

defend.time: why wrapping with modulo keeps enqueue and dequeue O(1)
defend.space: why it uses a fixed O(capacity) buffer

deque.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: each operation touches one end only, so adding or removing at either end is O(1).
deque.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the items; each operation needs O(1) extra.

contrast.point: one end only, so it can do half of what a deque does

defend.time: why adding and removing at both ends of a deque is O(1)
defend.space: what space it uses

singly-linked-list.worstCaseTrigger: Appending or finding the last node: with only a head pointer, every node is followed once, O(n). Work at the front is O(1); searching by value is O(n) on average too.
singly-linked-list.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the nodes, each with one extra pointer; traversal itself uses O(1).

contrast.point: O(1) access by index, but O(n) inserts at the front because of shifting

defend.time: why appending to a singly linked list without a tail pointer is O(n)
defend.remedy: how keeping a tail pointer makes it O(1)
defend.space: what memory each node costs compared with an array

doubly-linked-list.worstCaseTrigger: Searching for a value or reaching a middle position: nodes are walked one by one, O(n). With head and tail pointers, inserting or removing at either end is O(1).
doubly-linked-list.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the nodes, each with two pointers (next and prev), so more memory per node than a singly linked list.

contrast.point: one pointer per node, but no way to step backwards or delete a node without its predecessor

defend.time: why inserting at either end of a doubly linked list is O(1) but searching is O(n)
defend.space: what the extra prev pointer costs and buys

circular-linked-list.worstCaseTrigger: A search for a value that is not there: traversal goes all the way round to the starting node, O(n). Inserting next to the tail (with a tail pointer) is O(1).
circular-linked-list.auxiliarySpace: O(n) for the nodes; traversal uses O(1) and stops when it returns to where it began.

contrast.point: ends in null, so traversal stops there, but going round again means restarting from the head

defend.time: why a full traversal of a circular linked list is O(n) and how it knows when to stop
defend.space: what memory the list uses

array-access.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse: the address is base + index x element size, one calculation whatever the index or the array length, so access is O(1) every time.

contrast.point: reaching the i-th node means following i next pointers, O(n)

defend.time: why reading any index of an array is O(1)
defend.alternative: why a linked list cannot do the same
defend.space: what extra space an access needs

array-insert.worstCaseTrigger: Inserting at index 0: every one of the n elements shifts one place right, O(n). Inserting at the end shifts nothing, O(1); a random position shifts about n/2, still O(n).
array-insert.auxiliarySpace: O(1) extra: the shift happens in place (a full fixed-size array would need an O(n) copy into a larger one).

contrast.point: inserting after a node already in hand is O(1), with no shifting

defend.time: why inserting at the front of an array is O(n) but at the end is O(1)
defend.space: what extra space the shifting needs

array-delete.worstCaseTrigger: Deleting index 0: every element after it shifts one place left, O(n). Deleting the last element shifts nothing, O(1); a random position shifts about n/2, still O(n).
array-delete.auxiliarySpace: O(1) extra: the elements shift in place.

contrast.point: unlinking a node is O(1) once you hold the node before it

defend.time: why deleting the first element of an array is O(n) but the last is O(1)
defend.space: what extra space the shifting needs

hash-table-chaining.worstCaseTrigger: Every key hashing to the same bucket: one chain holds all n keys and a lookup scans it, O(n). A good hash spreading keys evenly keeps chains about n/capacity long, so the average is O(1) while the load factor stays low.
hash-table-chaining.auxiliarySpace: O(n + capacity): the buckets plus one chain entry per key.

contrast.point: no chains, but clusters form and probing slows as the table fills

defend.time: why lookups are O(1) on average but O(n) when every key collides
defend.remedy: how a good hash function and resizing keep chains short
defend.space: what space the buckets and chains take

hash-table-probing.worstCaseTrigger: Heavy clustering: as the table fills, occupied slots run together, so an insert or lookup probes along a long run, up to O(n). With a low load factor most probes stop after a slot or two, O(1) on average.
hash-table-probing.auxiliarySpace: O(capacity): one array of slots, no extra lists.

contrast.point: collisions go into per-bucket chains, so the table never fills, at the cost of the chain nodes

defend.time: why linear probing slows to O(n) as the load factor rises
defend.remedy: why keeping the load factor low (resizing) keeps it O(1)
defend.space: what space the table takes

sliding-window-variable.bestNote: each pointer moves at most n times
sliding-window-variable.worstNote: each pointer moves at most n times

jump-search.worstCaseTrigger: The target is absent or in the last block: it makes about √n jumps, then scans up to √n elements of a block, about 2√n checks, O(√n).
jump-search.auxiliarySpace: O(1): a jump size and two indices.

contrast.point: O(log n) on the same sorted array, but it jumps backwards through the range, which jump search avoids

defend.time: why a block size of √n gives O(√n)
defend.alternative: why binary search is still faster
defend.space: what extra space it needs

interpolation-search.worstCaseTrigger: Unevenly spread values: the position estimate keeps landing near one end, so each probe removes only a few elements, up to O(n). On uniformly spread values each estimate lands close, O(log log n) on average.
interpolation-search.auxiliarySpace: O(1): low, high and the probe index.

contrast.point: always halves, so a guaranteed O(log n) whatever the values

defend.time: why interpolation search is O(log log n) on uniform data but O(n) on skewed data
defend.space: what extra space it needs

exponential-search.worstCaseTrigger: A target near the end: the bound doubles about log i times to pass position i, then binary search covers a range of size about i, so O(log i), at most O(log n). A target near the start is found in a few steps.
exponential-search.auxiliarySpace: O(1) iteratively: the bound plus binary search's low, high and mid.

contrast.point: O(log n) over the whole array, while exponential search is O(log i) for a target at position i

defend.time: why exponential search is O(log i) for a target at position i
defend.alternative: when that beats plain binary search
defend.space: what extra space it needs

recursion-factorial.worstCaseTrigger: No input is worse for a given n: factorial(n) makes exactly n calls, each doing O(1) work, so it is O(n).
recursion-factorial.auxiliarySpace: O(n) stack frames: every call waits on the one below it until the base case returns.

contrast.point: the same O(n) time with O(1) space, since nothing waits on a stack

defend.time: why factorial makes n recursive calls
defend.space: why the recursion uses O(n) stack space and what a loop would use

recursion-fibonacci.worstCaseTrigger: Naive recursion: fib(n) calls fib(n - 1) and fib(n - 2), and each of those branches again, so the call tree roughly doubles each level, O(2ⁿ). The same values are recomputed many times.
recursion-fibonacci.auxiliarySpace: O(n) stack frames: only one path of the call tree, at most n calls deep, is on the stack at a time.

contrast.point: stores each value once, so O(n) time

defend.time: why naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ)
defend.remedy: how memoisation brings it down to O(n)
defend.space: why its stack is only O(n) deep
